name: Mulberry Purple
lede: Mulberry Purple is a dark, muted purple first recorded by Ridgway in 1912, and our library pairs it with Kikyō-iro, the Japanese traditional color named for the bellflower.

sections.title: Ridgway's plate and a bellflower's name
sections.body:
Our library's earliest record is Ridgway's 1912 color atlas, plate XI, hue 61 [1]. Maerz and Paul's 1930 dictionary repeats the name at plate 45, K10 [1]. The ISCC-NBS dictionary of 1955 filed it in block 224, "dark purple," 5.4 units from that block's centre [1]. Our library also pairs the English name with Kikyō-iro (桔梗色), the Japanese traditional color named for the bellflower, *Platycodon grandiflorus*; the flower reference does not match the English name's "mulberry," so the two naming traditions landed on this purple from different directions [1].

Its nearest named neighbor is [[cotinga-purple|Cotinga Purple]], 2.9 units away and read as almost the same color [2]. [[madder-violet|Madder Violet]] sits 3.8 units out, duller, and [[anthracene-violet|Anthracene Violet]] 4.3 units out, purpler [2]. Measured in LCH it reads lightness 33, chroma 32, a dark, muted purple [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this exact color in only 6 of 23,781 paintings (3 by the within-painting lens), rarer than 81 percent of the named colors, as photographed [3]. The sample is too thin here to say which painters or centuries favor it [3].

openers: Mulberry Purple's English name and its paired Japanese name, Kikyō-iro, point to two entirely different plants.
